claim: The thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) is a source for local, sensory-cortex-specific non-rapid-eye-movement sleep (NREMS) in mouse.
source: We identify the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) as a source for local, sensory-cortex-specific non-rapid-eye-movement sleep (NREMS) in mouse.
evidence: The abstract directly states this as a main finding of the study, supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Neurons in optogenetically identified sensory TRN sectors showed stronger repetitive burst discharge compared to non-sensory TRN cells.
source: Neurons in optogenetically identified sensory TRN sectors showed stronger repetitive burst discharge compared to non-sensory TRN cells due to higher activity of the low-threshold Ca2+ channel CaV3.3.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro electrophysiological recordings comparing burst discharge across TRN sectors, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: The stronger repetitive burst discharge in sensory TRN sectors is due to higher activity of the low-threshold Ca2+ channel CaV3.3.
source: Neurons in optogenetically identified sensory TRN sectors showed stronger repetitive burst discharge compared to non-sensory TRN cells due to higher activity of the low-threshold Ca2+ channel CaV3.3.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing WT and CaV3.3 KO animals, where genetic deletion of CaV3.3 abolished the differential burst propensity across sectors.

claim: Major NREMS rhythms in sensory but not non-sensory cortical areas were regulated in a CaV3.3-dependent manner.
source: Major NREMS rhythms in sensory but not non-sensory cortical areas were regulated in a CaV3.3-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo LFP recordings showing differential effects of CaV3.3 deletion on NREMS spectral properties across cortical areas (Figure 3).

claim: NREMS in somatosensory cortex was enriched in fast spindles.
source: In particular, NREMS in somatosensory cortex was enriched in fast spindles, but switched to delta wave-dominated sleep when CaV3.3 channels were genetically eliminated or somatosensory TRN cells chemogenetically hyperpolarized.
evidence: This is demonstrated by spindle detection analysis showing higher frequency and amplitude spindles in S1 and S2 of WT animals (Figure 5).

claim: NREMS in somatosensory cortex switched to delta wave-dominated sleep when CaV3.3 channels were genetically eliminated.
source: In particular, NREMS in somatosensory cortex was enriched in fast spindles, but switched to delta wave-dominated sleep when CaV3.3 channels were genetically eliminated or somatosensory TRN cells chemogenetically hyperpolarized.
evidence: Power spectral analysis shows increased delta power and decreased spindle power in S1 and S2 of CaV3.3 KO animals (Figure 3).

claim: NREMS in somatosensory cortex switched to delta wave-dominated sleep when somatosensory TRN cells were chemogenetically hyperpolarized.
source: In particular, NREMS in somatosensory cortex was enriched in fast spindles, but switched to delta wave-dominated sleep when CaV3.3 channels were genetically eliminated or somatosensory TRN cells chemogenetically hyperpolarized.
evidence: Chemogenetic inhibition of somatosensory TRN using CNO reproduced the spectral changes seen in CaV3.3 KO animals (Figure 4).

claim: TRN heterogeneity enables local sleep regulation according to use- and experience-dependence.
source: Our data indicate a previously unrecognized heterogeneity in a powerful forebrain oscillator that contributes to sensory-cortex-specific and dually regulated NREMS, enabling local sleep regulation according to use- and experience-dependence.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the demonstrated ability of TRN to switch between different NREMS rhythms and the known role of local sleep in experience-dependent plasticity.

claim: Sleep affects brain activity globally, but many cortical sleep waves are spatially confined.
source: Sleep affects brain activity globally, but many cortical sleep waves are spatially confined.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature on local sleep phenomena.

claim: Local rhythms serve cortical area-specific sleep needs and functions.
source: Local rhythms serve cortical area-specific sleep needs and functions; however, mechanisms controlling locality are unclear.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: Mechanisms controlling locality of sleep rhythms are unclear.
source: Local rhythms serve cortical area-specific sleep needs and functions; however, mechanisms controlling locality are unclear.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Cerebral correlates of NREMS and REMS occur variably at different times in different brain regions.
source: However, cerebral correlates of non-rapid-eye-movement sleep (NREMS) and REMS, notably several major EEG sleep rhythms, occur variably at different times in different brain regions (Massimini et al., 2004; Nir et al., 2011; Siclari and Tononi, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Forebrain pacemakers with regionally specific oscillatory properties shape sleep across the cortex.
source: This suggests that, on top of a global regulation, forebrain pacemakers with regionally specific oscillatory properties shape sleep across the cortex (Krueger et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of regional variability in sleep rhythms, supported by citation.

claim: Sleep-dependent memory consolidation is linked to spatially confined regulation of NREMS rhythms in brain areas involved in recent learning.
source: For example, sleep-dependent memory consolidation is linked to spatially confined regulation of NREMS rhythms in the brain areas involved in recent learning (Rasch and Born, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Sleep disorders may arise from pathologically altered spatial heterogeneity that negatively impacts sleep as a global state.
source: Furthermore, sleep disorders may arise from a pathologically altered spatial heterogeneity that negatively impacts sleep as a global state (Krueger et al., 2013; Siclari and Tononi, 2017).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Prototype cellular pacemakers for NREMS rhythms have been known for decades.
source: Prototype cellular pacemakers for NREMS rhythms, notably for the slow-oscillation (SO) (<1 Hz), delta waves (1–4 Hz) and sleep spindles (10–15 Hz) have been known for decades (for review, see (Steriade et al., 1993; Astori et al., 2013; Sanchez-Vives et al., 2017)).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by review citations.

claim: The spatiotemporal variability of cortical rhythms challenges the idea that pacemakers are homogeneous sources across the cortical surface.
source: However, the spatiotemporal variability of cortical rhythms challenges the idea that these are homogeneous sources across the cortical surface (Piantoni et al., 2016; Siclari and Tononi, 2017).
evidence: This is an inference from observations of variability, supported by citations.

claim: 'Fast' and 'slow' human sleep spindles distribute variably and correlate differentially with memory consolidation.
source: For example, 'fast' and 'slow' human sleep spindles distribute variably and correlate differentially with memory consolidation, which has prompted a search for at least two, if not several, separately active spindle generators (Schabus et al., 2007; Frauscher et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous human studies.

claim: Anatomical and functional boundaries of cortical areas go in parallel with variations of sleep rhythms.
source: Interestingly, anatomical and functional boundaries of cortical areas go in parallel with variations of sleep rhythms (Fernandez et al., 2017; Piantoni et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Sleep rhythms can show local singularities within a single cortical area according to developmental stage or as a result of experience and learning.
source: Moreover, sleep rhythms can show local singularities within a single cortical area according to developmental stage, or as a result of experience and learning during the day (Huber et al., 2004; Kurth et al., 2010; Johnson et al., 2012; Laventure et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: There is evidence for the localized appearance of sleep-related patterns in individual cortical columns.
source: There is also evidence for the localized appearance of sleep-related patterns in individual cortical columns (Pigarev et al., 1997; Rector et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Modality-specific thalamocortical loops could account for diversity in local NREMS.
source: Therefore, modality-specific thalamocortical loops could account for diversity in local NREMS.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the observations of local sleep variability.

claim: There should be powerful local tuning mechanisms to locally switch between different NREMS rhythms.
source: Moreover, there should be powerful local tuning mechanisms to locally switch between different NREMS rhythms.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the observation that different NREMS rhythms can occur locally.

claim: The current view is dominated by cortical focal influences as essential to shape local rhythms.
source: The current view is dominated by cortical focal influences as essential to shape local rhythms (Contreras et al., 1996; Piantoni et al., 2017; Siclari and Tononi, 2017).
evidence: This describes the prevailing view in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Thalamic oscillators are seen as broad and relatively homogeneous sources of oscillatory power.
source: In contrast, thalamic oscillators are seen as broad and relatively homogeneous sources of oscillatory power that can spread focally or globally to cortex (Bonjean et al., 2012), but that have little bearing on their ultimate cortical correlates.
evidence: This describes the traditional view of thalamic oscillators, supported by citation.

claim: Novel observations on heterogeneous thalamic pacemaker mechanisms are being reported.
source: This view is becoming revised as novel observations on heterogeneous thalamic pacemaker mechanisms are reported.
evidence: This indicates a shift in the field's understanding.

claim: The TRN is typically referred to as an inhibitory shell of highly oscillatory, burst-prone cells surrounding the dorsal thalamus.
source: Of interest is the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN), typically referred to as an inhibitory shell of highly oscillatory, burst-prone cells surrounding the dorsal thalamus (Pinault, 2004; Fogerson and Huguenard, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about TRN anatomy and function, supported by citations.

claim: TRN burst discharge generates large inhibitory synaptic potentials that entrain thalamocortical neurons into rhythmicity.
source: Burst discharge generates large inhibitory synaptic potentials (Herd et al., 2013; Rovó et al., 2014) that entrain thalamocortical neurons into rhythmicity.
evidence: This mechanism is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Bursting in TRN is based on the CaV3.3 channel that is crucial for sleep spindle generation.
source: Bursting is based on the CaV3.3 channel that is crucial for sleep spindle generation (Astori et al., 2011; Pellegrini et al., 2016), but many studies indicate that not all TRN cells burst equally (Contreras et al., 1992; Brunton and Charpak, 1997; Lee et al., 2007; Kimura et al., 2012; Clemente-Perez et al., 2017; Higashikubo and Moore, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Not all TRN cells burst equally.
source: Bursting is based on the CaV3.3 channel that is crucial for sleep spindle generation (Astori et al., 2011; Pellegrini et al., 2016), but many studies indicate that not all TRN cells burst equally (Contreras et al., 1992; Brunton and Charpak, 1997; Lee et al., 2007; Kimura et al., 2012; Clemente-Perez et al., 2017; Higashikubo and Moore, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies showing heterogeneity in TRN bursting.

claim: The TRN is parcellated into at least five modality-specific sectors.
source: Then, the TRN is parcellated into at least five modality-specific sectors, sensory, motor or limbic ones, according to their innervation by a particular dorsal thalamic nucleus and the reciprocally connected cortical area (Crabtree, 1999; Pinault, 2004).
evidence: This anatomical organization is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Optogenetic activation of TRN promotes cortical spindles or delta waves.
source: Moreover, optogenetic activation of TRN promotes cortical spindles or delta waves (Halassa et al., 2011; Lewis et al., 2015), suggesting that the exact patterns of TRN cell activity may determine the contribution of these two rhythms at the cortical surface.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous optogenetic studies.

claim: The exact patterns of TRN cell activity may determine the contribution of spindles and delta waves at the cortical surface.
source: Moreover, optogenetic activation of TRN promotes cortical spindles or delta waves (Halassa et al., 2011; Lewis et al., 2015), suggesting that the exact patterns of TRN cell activity may determine the contribution of these two rhythms at the cortical surface.
evidence: This is an inference from the optogenetic studies cited.

claim: Various discharge propensity in TRN cells was linked to the differential expression of parvalbumin (PV) or somatostatin.
source: Most recently, various discharge propensity in TRN cells was linked to the differential expression of parvalbumin (PV) or somatostatin (Clemente-Perez et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: The number of PV-expressing cells is smaller in TRN of schizophrenic patients and mouse models.
source: The number of PV-expressing cells is smaller in TRN of schizophrenic patients and mouse models (Steullet et al., 2018) in which reduced sleep spindle density is a common observation (Manoach et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on schizophrenia.

claim: Reduced sleep spindle density is a common observation in schizophrenic patients and mouse models.
source: The number of PV-expressing cells is smaller in TRN of schizophrenic patients and mouse models (Steullet et al., 2018) in which reduced sleep spindle density is a common observation (Manoach et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous studies.

claim: There is accruing evidence for marked molecular and functional TRN cell heterogeneity.
source: Together, there is accruing evidence for marked molecular and functional TRN cell heterogeneity.
evidence: This summarizes the evidence from multiple cited studies.

claim: Whether TRN heterogeneity is relevant for brain correlates of NREMS has not been tested.
source: However, whether TRN heterogeneity is relevant for brain correlates of NREMS has so far not been tested.
evidence: This identifies the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: AAV-ChR2_EYFP injections into S1 resulted in EYFP fluorescence in restricted portions of TRN corresponding to the somatosensory sector.
source: Enhanced yellow fluorescent protein (EYFP) fluorescence was present at injection sites and in restricted portions of TRN 3–4 weeks after injection, as verified on coronal sections stained immunohistochemically for PV to delineate the dorso-ventral extent of the TRN (Figure 1). The observed sectorial portions coincided with the ones established previously (Pinault and Deschênes, 1998; Pinault, 2004). Thus, injections into S1 revealed fibers navigating through the postero-dorsal portion of the TRN that terminated in elongated fluorescent spots in the thalamic ventral posterior medial nucleus corresponding to thalamic barreloids (Bourassa et al., 1995).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological verification shown in Figure 1 and matches previously established TRN anatomy.

claim: AAV-ChR2_EYFP injections into AC resulted in fluorescent labeling of postero-central regions of the TRN.
source: AC injections resulted in fluorescent labeling of postero-central regions of the TRN that are anterior to the medial geniculate nucleus.
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological verification shown in Figure 1.

claim: AAV-ChR2_EYFP injections into MD labeled antero-ventral portions of the TRN.
source: Finally, MD injections labeled antero-ventral portions of the TRN, overlapping with TRN areas innervating motor and intralaminar nuclei (Pinault and Deschênes, 1998; Pinault, 2004).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological verification shown in Figure 1 and matches previously established TRN anatomy.

claim: TRN cells recorded in green fluorescent areas reliably responded to optogenetic stimulation with rapid excitatory postsynaptic currents.
source: In acute coronal slices prepared from injected animals, TRN cells recorded in the green fluorescent areas through whole-cell patch clamp recordings reliably (> 85 % of the cells across sectors) responded to optogenetic stimulation (470 nm light, pulse duration ≤1 ms, 0.16 mW/mm2) with rapid excitatory postsynaptic currents ranging between -42 to -938 pA (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Paired stimuli yielded paired-pulse facilitation for cortical afferents to TRN.
source: Paired stimuli (interstimulus interval: 100 ms) yielded paired-pulse facilitation for cortical afferents (S1-innervated TRN cells: 203 ± 12%, n = 12, Wilcoxon signed rank-test, p=4.9x10−4 for 2nd vs 1st stimulus; for AC-innervated TRN cells: 175 ± 21%, n = 6, p=0.03), as described previously (Astori and Lüthi, 2013), whereas paired responses to MD stimulation showed comparable size (105 ± 4 %, n = 13, p=0.27).
evidence: This is demonstrated by paired-pulse recordings shown in Figure 2A with statistical analysis.

claim: Paired responses to MD stimulation showed comparable size between first and second stimulus.
source: Paired stimuli (interstimulus interval: 100 ms) yielded paired-pulse facilitation for cortical afferents (S1-innervated TRN cells: 203 ± 12%, n = 12, Wilcoxon signed rank-test, p=4.9x10−4 for 2nd vs 1st stimulus; for AC-innervated TRN cells: 175 ± 21%, n = 6, p=0.03), as described previously (Astori and Lüthi, 2013), whereas paired responses to MD stimulation showed comparable size (105 ± 4 %, n = 13, p=0.27).
evidence: This is demonstrated by paired-pulse recordings shown in Figure 2A with statistical analysis.

claim: S1- and AC-innervated TRN cells showed rhythmic, repetitive burst discharge.
source: S1- and AC-innervated TRN cells showed the rhythmic, repetitive burst discharge described previously (Figure 2C; Cueni et al., 2008; Astori et al., 2011), evident as several groups of high-frequency action potentials each riding on a triangular-shaped membrane depolarization and followed by a pronounced afterhyperpolarization.
evidence: This is demonstrated by current-clamp recordings shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Repetitive burst discharge strongly depended on the membrane voltage, showing an inverted U-shaped voltage dependence that peaked at -65 to -60 mV for S1-innervated cells.
source: Repetitive burst discharge strongly depended on the membrane voltage, showing an inverted U-shaped voltage dependence that peaked at -65 to -60 mV for S1-innervated cells (Figure 2D1,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by voltage-dependence analysis shown in Figure 2D1 and E.

claim: Only 1/12 S1-innervated TRN cells was a non-repetitive bursting cell.
source: Only 1/12 S1-innervated TRN cells was a non-repetitive bursting cell (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is shown in the histogram in Figure 2F.

claim: 4/13 AC-innervated TRN cells were non-repetitive bursters.
source: Similar burst propensity was found for TRN cells innervated from AC (Figure 2E), but 4/13 cells were non-repetitive bursters (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is shown in the histogram in Figure 2F.

claim: In MD-innervated TRN cells, repetitive bursting was weak and 9/14 cells discharged maximally one burst.
source: In TRN cells responding to MD inputs, repetitive bursting was weak (Figure 2C,D1) and 9/14 cells discharged maximally one burst (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by recordings and analysis shown in Figure 2C, D1, and F.

claim: Repetitive burst propensity is stronger in sensory compared to non-sensory TRN sectors.
source: These results show that repetitive burst propensity is stronger in sensory compared to non-sensory TRN sectors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative data across TRN sectors shown in Figure 2.

claim: Within sensory sectors, the somatosensory sector displayed the highest density of strongly bursting cells.
source: Within sensory sectors, the somatosensory sector displayed the highest density of strongly bursting cells, whereas the auditory sector had a smaller proportion of cells with rhythmic bursting.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparative analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The auditory TRN sector had a smaller proportion of cells with rhythmic bursting compared to the somatosensory sector.
source: Within sensory sectors, the somatosensory sector displayed the highest density of strongly bursting cells, whereas the auditory sector had a smaller proportion of cells with rhythmic bursting.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparative analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The vigorous bursting in somatosensory and auditory TRN cells was suppressed in CaV3.3 KO animals.
source: However, the vigorous bursting in somatosensory and auditory TRN cells was suppressed, thus abolishing the dependence of repetitive burst discharge propensity on TRN sector type (Kruskal-Wallis with factor 'sector', p=3×10−4 for WT, p=0.14 for CaV3.3 KO) (Figure 2D2, E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by recordings from CaV3.3 KO animals shown in Figure 2D2 and E.

claim: Genetic deletion of CaV3.3 abolished the dependence of repetitive burst discharge propensity on TRN sector type.
source: However, the vigorous bursting in somatosensory and auditory TRN cells was suppressed, thus abolishing the dependence of repetitive burst discharge propensity on TRN sector type (Kruskal-Wallis with factor 'sector', p=3×10−4 for WT, p=0.14 for CaV3.3 KO) (Figure 2D2, E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical comparison between WT and CaV3.3 KO shown in Figure 2D2 and E.

claim: The CaV3.3 channel endows superior bursting capacity to sensory over non-sensory TRN cells.
source: Together, these data indicate that the CaV3.3 channel endows superior bursting capacity to sensory over non-sensory TRN cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative data between WT and CaV3.3 KO animals across TRN sectors.

claim: NREMS in S1 and S2 showed prominent activity in the SO and sleep spindle frequency ranges in WT animals.
source: In S1 and S2, prominent activity in the SO (0.5–1.5 Hz, frequency band chosen based on visual inspection of the power spectrum) and the sleep spindle (sigma, 10–15 Hz) frequency ranges was visible (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by LFP recordings and power spectral analysis shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Activity in the delta frequency range was evident as large positive deflections in S1 and S2.
source: Activity in the delta (1.5–4 Hz) frequency range was evident as large positive deflections (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in filtered traces in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Similar, yet weaker rhythmic activity was observed in AC and PFC compared to S1 and S2.
source: Similar, yet weaker rhythmic activity was observed in AC and PFC.
evidence: This is evident from visual inspection of the traces in Figure 3C and power spectra in Figure 3D.

claim: The PFC showed signals dominated by slow events, including a component around 4 Hz resembling a respiratory-related rhythm.
source: The PFC showed signals dominated by slow events, as reported (Fernandez et al., 2017), which included a component around 4 Hz resembling a respiratory-related rhythm in frontal brain areas (Figure 3C,D; Zhong et al., 2017).
evidence: This is shown in the PFC traces and power spectra in Figure 3C and D, and supported by citations.

claim: A sigma power 'shoulder' was present only in somatosensory areas but not in AC and PFC.
source: Power spectral analyses over total NREMS times of 2200–6100 s per animal (average 4487 ± 603 s, concatenated from NREMS bouts across recording days) showed that NREMS in all recorded areas had broadly elevated power in the low-frequency range covering both the SO and the delta range (0.5–4 Hz), whereas a 'shoulder' in the sigma band was present only in somatosensory areas (n = 9 for S1 and n = 8 for S2) but not in AC (n = 6) and PFC (n = 6) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by power spectral analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There was a striking lack of visually recognizable sleep spindle activity in S1 and S2 of CaV3.3 KO animals.
source: NREMS in animals lacking CaV3.3 channels showed several marked changes that were apparent in both the raw traces and in characteristic alterations of the power spectra (NREMS recording times of 1800–7000 s per animal, average 3459 ± 421 s). First, there was a striking lack of visually recognizable sleep spindle activity in S1 and S2, and a sigma power shoulder was not present in the power spectrum (Figure 3C,D, bottom panel showing enlarged portions of the power spectrum and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in the raw traces and power spectra in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Activity in the delta range was augmented in S1, S2, and AC of CaV3.3 KO animals, whereas the SO was less prominent.
source: Second, activity in the delta range was augmented, whereas the SO was less prominent in LFP traces from S1, S2 and AC.
evidence: This is evident from the raw traces and power spectra shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The power spectra for WT and CaV3.3 KO animals intersected in the slow frequencies around 1.6–1.8 Hz for S1, S2 and AC.
source: The power spectra for WT and CaV3.3 KO animals intersected in the slow frequencies around 1.6–1.8 Hz for S1, S2 and AC, suggesting a consistent spectral border between the SO and the delta bands.
evidence: This is shown in the power spectra in Figure 3D.

claim: In PFC, no alterations in the power spectrum were observed in CaV3.3 KO animals, with no significant change in the sigma power and in the SO peak.
source: In PFC, in contrast, no alterations in the power spectrum were observed, with in particular no significant change in the sigma power and in the SO peak.
evidence: This is shown in the power spectra and quantification in Figure 3D and E.

claim: The lack of CaV3.3 channels altered the spectral mix of NREMS in sensory circuits, whereby power in the delta frequency band became overrepresented compared to the SO.
source: Together, the lack of CaV3.3 channels altered the spectral mix of NREMS in sensory circuits, whereby power in the delta frequency band became overrepresented compared to the SO.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the power spectral analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The shift in spectral mix was greatest in S1 and S2, where sigma power activity was also suppressed.
source: This shift was greatest in S1 and S2, where in addition sigma power activity was suppressed.
evidence: This is evident from the quantification in Figure 3E.

claim: Bath application of CNO induced a marked membrane hyperpolarization in fluorescent TRN cells expressing hM4Di.
source: In acute slices prepared 3 weeks after injection, bath application of the DREADD-ligand Clozapine N-oxide (CNO, 10 μM) induced a marked membrane hyperpolarization (ΔV = −13.9 ± 1.5 mV, n = 10, paired t-test, p=6×10−6) of fluorescent cells held in whole-cell current-clamp at resting membrane potentials ranging from −50 to −70 mV (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro recordings shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: CNO application reduced cellular input resistance and suppressed rebound burst discharge in hM4Di-expressing TRN cells.
source: Cellular input resistance was reduced and rebound burst discharge suppressed in the continuous presence of CNO.
evidence: This is shown in the recordings in Figure 4A.

claim: Bursting could be recovered upon direct current injection to restore the original membrane potential in CNO-treated hM4Di-expressing TRN cells.
source: Bursting could be recovered upon direct current (d.c.) injection to restore the original membrane potential (d.c. injection tested in n = 3 cells, Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4A.

claim: Non-fluorescent cells in the vicinity of the injected area did not respond to CNO.
source: Non-fluorescent cells in the vicinity of the injected area did not respond to CNO (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 4B.

claim: CNO-induced activation of K+ conductances silences TRN neurons without impairing rebound bursting and action potential firing.
source: This result is consistent with CNO-induced activation of K+ conductances and shows that TRN neurons become silenced without impairing rebound bursting and action potential firing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the CNO effects based on known DREADD mechanisms and the observation that bursting can be restored with current injection.

claim: CNO treatment specifically reproduces the decreased burst propensity of TRN cells found in CaV3.3-KO animals.
source: Treatment with CNO thus overall reduces TRN excitability, and in particular specifically reproduces the decreased burst propensity of TRN cells found in the CaV3.3-KO animals that is relevant for the altered NREMS spectral properties.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the effects of CNO with those observed in CaV3.3 KO animals.

claim: The latencies to fall asleep were comparable after CNO or NaCl injections in vivo.
source: The latencies to fall asleep were comparable after drug or NaCl injections (31.4 ± 3.7 min for CNO, 24.8 ± 2.1 min for NaCl; n = 5, paired t-test, p=0.16).
evidence: This is based on behavioral analysis of sleep onset after injections.

claim: Total time spent in NREMS was not different between CNO and NaCl injections in the analysis period.
source: Total time spent in NREMS was not different between CNO and NaCl injections in the analysis period (24.1 ± 1.7 min for CNO, 27.7 ± 1.9 min for NaCl injections, Wilcoxon signed rank-test, p=0.22) and mean NREMS bout durations were comparable (93.3 ± 12.3 s for CNO, 91.2 ± 32.5 s for NaCl, Wilcoxon signed rank-test, p=0.31).
evidence: This is based on sleep scoring analysis.

claim: Following CNO injections, S1 LFP signals during NREMS showed reduced spindle activity and became enriched in activity in the delta frequency range.
source: Following CNO injections, S1 LFP signals during NREMS showed reduced spindle activity and instead became enriched in activity in the delta frequency range (Figure 4C,D, repeated-measures ANOVA with factors 'frequency' and 'treatment', p=7.7×10−5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vivo LFP recordings and power spectral analysis shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Compared to NaCl injections, CNO increased total power in the delta frequency range and suppressed SO and spindle activity in S1.
source: Compared to NaCl injections, total power in the delta frequency range was increased, whereas the SO and spindle activity were suppressed (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This is shown in the power spectral analysis and quantification in Figure 4D and E.

claim: Control animals injected with AAV8 carrying a DREADD-unrelated optogenetic construct did not respond to CNO.
source: Control animals injected with AAV8 carrying a DREADD-unrelated optogenetic construct (see Materials and methods) did not respond to CNO (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–F.

claim: CNO-induced acute membrane hyperpolarization reproduced the major power spectral changes observed in NREMS of the CaV3.3 KO mouse.
source: The CNO-induced acute membrane hyperpolarization thus reproduced the major power spectral changes observed in NREMS of the CaV3.3 KO mouse: the suppression of the SO and sleep spindle power, and the enhancement of delta power.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the chemogenetic results with the genetic knockout results.

claim: Decreased TRN bursting is the primary factor relevant for the enrichment of delta power at the expense of sigma and SO power in NREMS.
source: As CNO-induced hyperpolarization suppressed burst discharge (see also Figure 2D1), the joint results from the genetic and the chemogenetic manipulations identify decreased TRN bursting as the primary factor relevant for the enrichment of delta power at the expense of sigma and SO power in NREMS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined results of genetic and chemogenetic manipulations.

claim: Spindles in S1 and S2 showed large amplitudes that were comparable to that of the SO in WT animals.
source: Spindles in S1 and S2 showed large amplitudes that were comparable to that of the SO, whereas those in AC and PFC were less prominent (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in the representative traces in Figure 5A.

claim: In CaV3.3 KO animals, the large spindle events were reduced in S1 and S2, but remained comparable in AC.
source: In the CaV3.3 KO animals, the large spindle events were reduced in S1 and S2, but remained comparable in AC.
evidence: This is shown in the amplitude analysis in Figure 5B.

claim: There was a reduction of spindle event amplitude in PFC of CaV3.3 KO animals.
source: There was also a reduction of event amplitude in PFC (Figure 5B1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B1.

claim: Cumulative probability density curves showed a marked leftward shift of the amplitude distribution in S1 and S2, but not in AC and PFC of CaV3.3 KO animals.
source: Cumulative probability density curves showed a marked leftward shift of the amplitude distribution in S1 and S2, but not in AC and PFC (Figure 5B2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B2.

claim: The frequency of detected spindle events was distributed according to a Gaussian between 9 and 16 Hz, with a maximum around 10–12 Hz in WT animals.
source: The frequency of detected events was distributed according to a Gaussian between 9 and 16 Hz, with a maximum around 10–12 Hz, yielding means of 11.6 ± 0.09 Hz for S1; 11.7 ± 0.05 Hz for S2; 11.2 ± 0.05 Hz for AC; 11.5 ± 0.03 Hz for PFC (Figure 5C1).
evidence: This is shown in the frequency distribution analysis in Figure 5C1.

claim: All spindle frequency distributions showed a tail indicating a small proportion of events with a frequency >14 Hz.
source: All distributions showed a tail indicating a small proportion of events with a frequency >14 Hz (Figure 5C2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C2.

claim: In CaV3.3 KO animals, spindle frequencies were specifically attenuated in S1 and S2, but remained comparable in AC and PFC.
source: In the CaV3.3 KO animals, frequencies were specifically attenuated in S1 and S2, but remained comparable in AC and PFC.
evidence: This is shown in the frequency analysis in Figure 5C.

claim: The greater activity of CaV3.3 channels in the sensory sectors of TRN correlated strongly with higher amplitudes and frequencies of individual spindles in S1 and S2.
source: The greater activity of CaV3.3 channels in the sensory sectors of TRN thus correlated strongly with higher amplitudes and frequencies of individual spindles in S1 and S2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spindle analysis comparing WT and CaV3.3 KO animals.

claim: Sleep spindles are temporally grouped by the active state of the SO.
source: Sleep spindles are temporally grouped by the active state of the SO, which reflects the strong role of corticothalamic volleys in recruiting thalamic circuits (Contreras et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The grouping of spindles by the SO is key for the promotion of sleep-dependent memory consolidation.
source: This grouping is key for the promotion of sleep-dependent memory consolidation (Mölle et al., 2009) and it may be disrupted in some cases of schizophrenia (Manoach et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The grouping of spindles by the SO may be disrupted in some cases of schizophrenia.
source: This grouping is key for the promotion of sleep-dependent memory consolidation (Mölle et al., 2009) and it may be disrupted in some cases of schizophrenia (Manoach et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Approximately 60% and 40% of detected spindles initiated during the cortical active and silent states, respectively, in WT animals across all areas.
source: We determined the onset times of detected spindles with respect to the phase of the SO (Figure 6A) and confirmed such time-locking throughout all areas, with ~60% and 40% of detected spindles initiating during the cortical active and silent states (also named UP and DOWN states), respectively (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is shown in the phase-locking analysis in Figure 6B and C.

claim: The time-locking of sleep spindles to the SO was altered for S1 and S2 in CaV3.3 KO animals, but not for AC and PFC.
source: Remarkably, the same analysis in the CaV3.3 KO animals showed that the time-locking of sleep spindles to the SO was altered for S1 and S2 (Figure 6B,C), but not for AC and PFC.
evidence: This is shown in the phase-locking analysis in Figure 6B and C.

claim: In S1 and S2 of CaV3.3 KO animals, the presence of spindles on the active state was diminished in favor of spindles in the silent state.
source: In both S1 and S2, the presence of spindles on the active state was diminished in favor of spindles in the silent state.
evidence: This is shown in the phase-locking analysis in Figure 6C.

claim: In S1 from CaV3.3 KO animals, the occurrence of spindles was comparable between active and silent states.
source: In S1 from CaV3.3 KO animals, the occurrence of spindles was comparable between active and silent states, whereas events occurred preferentially in the silent state in S2.
evidence: This is shown in the phase-locking analysis in Figure 6C.

claim: In S2 from CaV3.3 KO animals, spindle events occurred preferentially in the silent state.
source: In S1 from CaV3.3 KO animals, the occurrence of spindles was comparable between active and silent states, whereas events occurred preferentially in the silent state in S2.
evidence: This is shown in the phase-locking analysis in Figure 6C.

claim: The presence of CaV3.3 ensures the timely occurrence of sleep spindles with respect to the cortical active state.
source: Therefore, the presence of CaV3.3 ensures the timely occurrence of sleep spindles with respect to the cortical active state.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the phase-locking analysis comparing WT and CaV3.3 KO animals.

claim: Sectorial attributes of TRN circuits emerge as a powerful source for local NREMS correlates.
source: Sectorial attributes of TRN circuits thus emerge as a powerful source for local NREMS correlates.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study based on the combined in vitro and in vivo data.

claim: TRN sectorial attributes facilitate a tuning of NREMS between major spectral correlates.
source: They additionally facilitate a tuning of NREMS between major spectral correlates, offering a candidate mechanism for local sleep modulation, possibly in response to use, experience and learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the demonstrated ability to switch between spindle- and delta-dominated NREMS.

claim: A sectorial heterogeneity of TRN will advance insight into a proposed common vulnerability of TRN circuitry for both sleep and wakefulness-driven selective attention in neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: A sectorial heterogeneity of TRN will also advance insight into a proposed common vulnerability of TRN circuitry for both sleep as well as wakefulness-driven selective attention in neuropsychiatric disorders (Krol et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculation about the broader implications of the findings, supported by citation.

claim: The TRN has been traditionally regarded as a homogeneous sleep rhythm pacemaker.
source: The TRN has been traditionally regarded as a homogeneous sleep rhythm pacemaker (Fuentealba and Steriade, 2005; Fogerson and Huguenard, 2016) that underlies global thalamic inhibition (Halassa and Acsády, 2016).
evidence: This describes the traditional view, supported by citations.

claim: The molecular and functional heterogeneity of TRN is increasingly recognized.
source: Although its molecular and functional heterogeneity is increasingly recognized, consequences for NREMS are so far poorly explored and the role of sector-specific TRN cell characteristics is unknown.
evidence: This describes the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Consequences of TRN heterogeneity for NREMS are poorly explored.
source: Although its molecular and functional heterogeneity is increasingly recognized, consequences for NREMS are so far poorly explored and the role of sector-specific TRN cell characteristics is unknown.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge.

claim: The role of sector-specific TRN cell characteristics for NREMS is unknown.
source: Although its molecular and functional heterogeneity is increasingly recognized, consequences for NREMS are so far poorly explored and the role of sector-specific TRN cell characteristics is unknown.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: It is not clear whether heterogeneous cellular discharge properties in TRN are important for local sleep.
source: Thus, it is not clear whether heterogeneous cellular discharge properties (Contreras et al., 1992; Brunton and Charpak, 1997; Lee et al., 2007; Kimura et al., 2012; Higashikubo and Moore, 2018) or variable expression of PV and somatostatin are important for local sleep (Clemente-Perez et al., 2017).
evidence: This identifies an open question in the field.

claim: Sensory but not limbic TRN cells preferentially engage in sleep-related activity.
source: Furthermore, sensory but not limbic TRN cells preferentially engage in sleep-related activity (Halassa et al., 2014), but it is not known whether they are cellularly distinct.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: It is not known whether sensory and limbic TRN cells are cellularly distinct.
source: Furthermore, sensory but not limbic TRN cells preferentially engage in sleep-related activity (Halassa et al., 2014), but it is not known whether they are cellularly distinct.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge.

claim: This study is the first to bring together TRN heterogeneities at both the in vitro and the in vivo levels using optogenetically assisted mapping of TRN sectors.
source: Therefore, this study is the first to bring together TRN heterogeneities at both the in vitro and the in vivo levels using optogenetically assisted mapping of TRN sectors.
evidence: This describes the novelty of the study's approach.

claim: Cellular heterogeneities align with identified TRN sectors, and TRN sectors with area-specific NREMS.
source: We show that cellular heterogeneities align with identified TRN sectors, and TRN sectors with area-specific NREMS, thus establishing the TRN sector-specific cellular properties as a source for local and tunable NREMS.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study based on the combined data.

claim: PV-positive cells are stronger bursters than cells enriched in somatostatin.
source: Based on a previous study demonstrating that PV-positive cells are stronger bursters than cells enriched in somatostatin (Clemente-Perez et al., 2017), we propose that PV-positive TRN cells are primary determinants of the unique sleep spindle properties in somatosensory cortex.
evidence: This is based on citation to a previous study.

claim: PV-positive TRN cells are primary determinants of the unique sleep spindle properties in somatosensory cortex.
source: Based on a previous study demonstrating that PV-positive cells are stronger bursters than cells enriched in somatostatin (Clemente-Perez et al., 2017), we propose that PV-positive TRN cells are primary determinants of the unique sleep spindle properties in somatosensory cortex.
evidence: This is a proposal based on inference from the current findings and previous literature.

claim: Somatosensory cortices showed a clear sigma power 'shoulder' and strong, fast, CaV3.3-dependent spindle events.
source: One remarkable observation is that somatosensory cortices showed a clear sigma power 'shoulder' and strong, fast, CaV3.3-dependent spindle events.
evidence: This is based on the power spectral and spindle analysis shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: The widespread idea from EEG recordings that sleep spindle generation in mouse NREMS is weak should be revised.
source: The widespread idea from EEG recordings that sleep spindle generation in mouse NREMS is weak (Astori et al., 2011) should thus be revised as we now show that full-fledged spindle activity is generated in local regions of the mouse brain.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the demonstration of strong local spindles in S1 and S2.

claim: Full-fledged spindle activity is generated in local regions of the mouse brain.
source: The widespread idea from EEG recordings that sleep spindle generation in mouse NREMS is weak (Astori et al., 2011) should thus be revised as we now show that full-fledged spindle activity is generated in local regions of the mouse brain.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the spindle analysis in S1 and S2 shown in Figure 5.

claim: The highly focal synaptic organization of the barrel system is likely an important anatomical substrate enabling strong local spindles.
source: The highly focal synaptic organization of the barrel system, where TRN-thalamic, thalamocortical and corticothalamic projections between barreloid and barrel topographically match on a cell-to-cell basis (Desîlets-Roy et al., 2002; Wimmer et al., 2010), together with a high density of PV-positive, bursty cells in the TRN somatosensory sector (Clemente-Perez et al., 2017), are likely important anatomical substrates enabling strong local spindles.
evidence: This is a speculation based on known anatomy and the current findings, supported by citations.

claim: A high density of PV-positive, bursty cells in the TRN somatosensory sector is likely an important anatomical substrate enabling strong local spindles.
source: The highly focal synaptic organization of the barrel system, where TRN-thalamic, thalamocortical and corticothalamic projections between barreloid and barrel topographically match on a cell-to-cell basis (Desîlets-Roy et al., 2002; Wimmer et al., 2010), together with a high density of PV-positive, bursty cells in the TRN somatosensory sector (Clemente-Perez et al., 2017), are likely important anatomical substrates enabling strong local spindles.
evidence: This is a speculation based on known anatomy and the current findings, supported by citations.

claim: The tight alignment of thalamic unit and S1 LFP activity recorded simultaneously during spindles in urethane anaesthesia supports the interpretation that anatomical substrates enable strong local spindles.
source: The tight alignment of thalamic unit and S1 LFP activity recorded simultaneously during spindles in urethane anaesthesia (Rovó et al., 2014) supports this interpretation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Prominent sigma power and high-amplitude spindles were observed in S2 that exceeded levels in S1.
source: We also observed prominent sigma power and high-amplitude spindles in S2 that exceeded levels in S1.
evidence: This is shown in the power spectral and spindle analysis in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: High reciprocal cortical connectivity between S1 and S2 could be a reason for the difference in spindle properties between S1 and S2.
source: High reciprocal cortical connectivity between S1 and S2 (Feldmeyer et al., 2013), and a differential recruitment of first- and higher order thalamic nuclei in these two areas, could be some of the reasons behind this difference.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanisms underlying the observed differences, supported by citation.

claim: Differential recruitment of first- and higher order thalamic nuclei in S1 and S2 could be a reason for the difference in spindle properties.
source: High reciprocal cortical connectivity between S1 and S2 (Feldmeyer et al., 2013), and a differential recruitment of first- and higher order thalamic nuclei in these two areas, could be some of the reasons behind this difference.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanisms underlying the observed differences.

claim: No discernable sigma power shoulder was present in AC.
source: In contrast to S1 and S2, no discernable sigma power shoulder was present in AC, and detected spindles showed no dependence on the CaV3.3 channel.
evidence: This is shown in the power spectral analysis in Figure 3D.

claim: Detected spindles in AC showed no dependence on the CaV3.3 channel.
source: In contrast to S1 and S2, no discernable sigma power shoulder was present in AC, and detected spindles showed no dependence on the CaV3.3 channel.
evidence: This is shown in the spindle analysis in Figure 5.

claim: There was a tendency for a decreased density of highly burst-prone cells in the auditory TRN sector in mouse.
source: We found a tendency for a decreased density of highly burst-prone cells in mouse, which possibly reduces the strength of spindle generation in auditory sectors.
evidence: This is based on the in vitro recordings shown in Figure 2.

claim: The spectral composition of NREMS in pre- and infralimbic portions of the PFC showed no prominent sigma power and no overall dependence on CaV3.3 channels.
source: Similarly, the spectral composition of NREMS in pre- and infralimbic portions of the PFC showed no prominent sigma power and no overall dependence on CaV3.3 channels, consistent with a minor expression of CaV3.3 channels in the MD-innervated sector and with the presence of a majority of somatostatin-positive, weakly bursting cells in these areas of the TRN (Clemente-Perez et al., 2017).
evidence: This is shown in the power spectral analysis in Figure 3 and is consistent with the in vitro findings and previous literature.

claim: Discrete spindles could be detected in mouse PFC.
source: However, discrete spindles could be detected in mouse and they are well-described for rat PFC (Siapas and Wilson, 1998; Peyrache et al., 2011; Maingret et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on the spindle detection analysis and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Discrete spindle events in PFC were accompanied by a phase entrainment of TRN discharge in sleeping rats.
source: Discrete spindle events were accompanied by a phase entrainment of TRN discharge in sleeping rats, although mean firing rates seemed low (Gardner et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: There could be a spindle-generating circuitry independent of the powerful CaV3.3-dependent mechanisms in sensory TC loops, in which anterior and midline thalamic nuclei and hippocampus are involved.
source: There could thus be a spindle-generating circuitry independent of the powerful CaV3.3-dependent mechanisms in sensory TC loops, in which anterior and midline thalamic nuclei and hippocampus are involved.
evidence: This is a speculation about alternative spindle-generating mechanisms.

claim: Power in the SO band was consistently co-modulated with sleep spindle activity in both the CaV3.3 KO mouse and during chemogenetic TRN inhibition.
source: Power in the SO band was consistently co-modulated with sleep spindle activity in both the CaV3.3 KO mouse and during chemogenetic TRN inhibition.
evidence: This is shown in the power spectral analyses in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The co-modulation of SO and spindle power could be evidence in favor of a role of TRN in the generation of the SO.
source: This could be evidence in favor of a role of TRN in the generation of the SO (Crunelli et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed co-modulation, supported by citation.

claim: The chemogenetic results support the idea that the TRN sustains low-frequency activity in cortico-thalamocortical loops.
source: Our chemogenetic results generally support the idea that the TRN sustains low-frequency activity in cortico-thalamocortical loops, an effect which could possibly also result secondarily from its phasic recruitment by cortex to generate sleep spindles.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the chemogenetic results.

claim: The increase of delta power could have de-emphasized the relative presence of SOs.
source: Also, the increase of delta power could have de-emphasized the relative presence of SOs.
evidence: This is a speculation about the interpretation of the power spectral changes.

claim: Possible roles of CaV3.3 channels in cortically generated rhythms could arise from a subgroup of cortical interneurons.
source: Additionally, possible roles of CaV3.3 channels in cortically generated rhythms could arise from a subgroup of cortical interneurons (Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculation about alternative mechanisms, supported by citation.

claim: The genetic removal of the CaV3.3 channel enhanced delta power in S1 and S2 at the expense of sleep spindles.
source: The genetic removal of the CaV3.3 channel enhanced delta power in S1 and S2 at the expense of sleep spindles.
evidence: This is shown in the power spectral analysis in Figure 3.

claim: Chemogenetic hyperpolarization reproduced the observation of enhanced delta power at the expense of spindles.
source: Chemogenetic hyperpolarization reproduced this observation closely.
evidence: This is shown in the chemogenetic experiments in Figure 4.

claim: Suppressed bursting is the principal mechanism involved in the effects of CaV3.3 deletion and chemogenetic hyperpolarization on NREMS.
source: Although the chemogenetic approach suppresses excitability in a manner that is not limited to bursting, the close correspondence with the observations in the CaV3.3-KO animals, in which only bursting but not tonic firing is impaired (Astori et al., 2011), strongly suggests that suppressed bursting, which is the common denominator of both experimental approaches, is the principal mechanism involved in the effects at the level of NREMS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the genetic and chemogenetic results.

claim: An enhancement and/or unmasking of delta wave-generating activity in thalamocortical circuits has become apparent thanks to the locality of the recordings.
source: While the reduction in sleep spindle activity under these conditions is expected (Astori et al., 2011), an enhancement and/or unmasking of delta wave-generating activity in thalamocortical circuits has now become apparent thanks to the locality of our recordings.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the local LFP recordings showing increased delta power.

claim: The enhancement of delta power is reminiscent of previous observations of an opposite regulation of slow wave/delta and spindle power during NREMS.
source: It is reminiscent of previous observations of an opposite regulation of slow wave/delta and spindle power during NREMS (Dijk et al., 1993; Steriade et al., 1993; Franken et al., 1998), which has been explained based on the different membrane potential polarizations of TC cells involved in spindle or delta rhythm generation (Nuñez et al., 1992).
evidence: This connects the current findings to previous literature, supported by citations.

claim: TRN cell membrane potential polarization is a determinant for the regulation of spindle versus delta rhythms in somatosensory thalamocortical circuits during NREMS.
source: Here, we identify TRN cell membrane potential polarization as a determinant for such regulation in somatosensory thalamocortical circuits during NREMS.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study based on the combined genetic and chemogenetic results.

claim: The capability of TRN in generating either spindles or delta waves was evident based on whether brief or prolonged optogenetic stimulation was applied.
source: Remarkably, the capability of TRN in generating either spindles or delta waves was also evident based on whether brief or prolonged optogenetic stimulation was applied (Halassa et al., 2011; Lewis et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous optogenetic studies.

claim: TRN-dependent inhibition has power in controlling thalamocortical synchrony according to discharge patterns.
source: This underscores the power of TRN-dependent inhibition in controlling thalamocortical synchrony according to discharge patterns.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the current findings and previous optogenetic studies.

claim: TRN hyperpolarization liberates TC cells from phasic hyperpolarization to engage in a clock-like rhythm at delta frequencies.
source: In agreement with pioneering work on delta waves, we propose that TRN hyperpolarization liberates TC cells from phasic hyperpolarization to engage in a clock-like rhythm at delta frequencies (Steriade et al., 1993).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the current findings and previous literature, supported by citation.

claim: Results consistent with the interpretation that TRN hyperpolarization liberates TC cells were obtained in animals doubly deficient in CaV3 channels.
source: Results consistent with this interpretation were also obtained in animals doubly deficient in CaV3 channels (Pellegrini et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of anterior TRN cells may suppress rather than strengthen low-frequency EEG activity.
source: Recently, it was also shown that optogenetic inhibition of anterior TRN cells may suppress rather than strengthen low-frequency EEG activity (Herrera et al., 2016), yet this effect occurred with a 10-s-long delay after acute inhibition of TRN cell discharge.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The powerful control of delta power by TRN-dependent mechanism could be relevant for the role of delta waves in the homeostatic regulation of NREMS.
source: The powerful control of delta power by TRN-dependent mechanism could be relevant for the role of delta waves in the homeostatic regulation of NREMS.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional implications of the findings.

claim: The increase in low-frequency power of NREMS over the 0.75–4 Hz power band, referred to as slow-wave activity, is the most widely used marker to quantify homeostatic sleep pressure.
source: The increase in low-frequency power of NREMS over the 0.75–4 Hz power band, referred to as slow-wave activity, is the most widely used marker to quantify homeostatic sleep pressure (Borbély and Tobler, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Slow-wave activity contains a thalamically controlled component that can be rapidly and bidirectionally modulated through TRN membrane polarization.
source: We find here that slow-wave activity contains a thalamically controlled component that can be rapidly and bidirectionally modulated through TRN membrane polarization.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the demonstrated effects of TRN manipulation on delta power.

claim: TRN-dependent mechanisms could contribute to sleep-deprivation induced boosting of the high- but not the low-frequency component of slow-wave activity.
source: Such mechanisms could contribute to sleep-deprivation induced boosting of the high- but not the low-frequency component of slow-wave activity (Achermann and Borbély, 1997; Huber et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a speculation about how the findings relate to sleep homeostasis, supported by citations.

claim: Bidirectional regulation of slow-wave activity in local brain areas according to use dependence has been described.
source: Bidirectional regulation of slow-wave activity in local brain areas according to use dependence has also been described (Kattler et al., 1994; Pigarev et al., 1997; Vyazovskiy et al., 2000; Miyamoto and Hensch, 2003; Huber et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: More complex localized alterations in NREMS are observed following exposure to learning tasks that involve enhanced power in both the low-frequency range and in the fast sleep spindle range.
source: More complex localized alterations in NREMS are observed following exposure to learning tasks that involve enhanced power in both the low-frequency range (SO and delta waves in the slow wave activity frequency range of 0.5–4 Hz) and in the fast sleep spindle range (Huber et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Learning tasks involving motor cortex increase the density of individual spindle events in a manner specifically restricted to motor cortex.
source: Learning tasks involving motor cortex increase the density of individual spindle events in a manner specifically restricted to motor cortex (Johnson et al., 2012) or augmented both slow wave and sleep spindle power in supplementary motor cortex (Tamaki et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cortical modules are capable of generating qualitatively different forms of local NREMS spontaneously and according to recent use and experience.
source: Therefore, cortical modules are capable of generating qualitatively different forms of local NREMS spontaneously and according to recent use and experience.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cited literature on use-dependent sleep regulation.

claim: Membrane potential polarization within TRN sectors could represent a powerful addition to previously proposed mechanisms that primarily imply changes in cortical synaptic strength.
source: Membrane potential polarization within TRN sectors could represent a powerful addition to previously proposed mechanisms that primarily imply changes in cortical synaptic strength (Tononi and Cirelli, 2014).
evidence: This is a speculation about how the findings complement existing theories, supported by citation.

claim: Ascending brainstem and basal forebrain as well as descending cortical inputs regulate TRN membrane potential and burst propensity.
source: Both ascending brainstem and basal forebrain (McCormick and Bal, 1997; Beierlein, 2014) as well as descending cortical inputs (McCormick and von Krosigk, 1992; Zhang et al., 2012) regulate TRN membrane potential and burst propensity.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Whether differential neuromodulation of TRN sectors contributes to use- and experience-dependent sleep regulation remains an intriguing topic for further study.
source: Whether differential neuromodulation of TRN sectors contributes to use- and experience-dependent sleep regulation remains an intriguing topic for further study.
evidence: This identifies a future research direction.

claim: Compromised sleep spindle generation is a promising read-out for neuropsychiatric disorders involving aberrant sensory percepts and attentional deficits, such as schizophrenia.
source: Compromised sleep spindle generation is a promising read-out for neuropsychiatric disorders involving aberrant sensory percepts and attentional deficits, such as schizophrenia (Manoach et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on schizophrenia.

claim: The gene encoding CaV3.3 channels ranks in the top list of candidate risk genes in schizophrenia.
source: In large-scale genome-wide association studies, the gene encoding CaV3.3 channels ranks in the top list of candidate risk genes in schizophrenia, together with several genes that are highly enriched in TRN and implied in repetitive burst discharge (Krol et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Wake-related deficits in some schizophrenia patients may show a specificity for certain sensory modalities that co-vary with local deficits in sleep spindles and their coupling to the SO.
source: Based on our data, we propose that wake-related deficits in some of these patients may show a specificity for certain sensory modalities that co-vary with local deficits in sleep spindles and their coupling to the SO.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the current findings and their potential implications for schizophrenia.

claim: Modality-specific deficits in schizophrenia could help to further refine the classification and diagnosis of these complex disorders.
source: This could help to further refine the classification and diagnosis of these complex disorders.
evidence: This is a speculation about the clinical implications of the findings.
